column4: After every conversation, a number appears over the other person's head. How much they actually liked talking to you. Out of ten.
And in your head, there's another number. Your guess.
Five minutes with Juno. You're already sure it went badly.
The "you too." The weird laugh. The goodbye.
You give yourself a two.
She gave you a nine.
That can't be right. So you test it.
Mo. You guess three.
Finn. You guess four.
Bea. You guess two.
Every single time, you guess low.
After a conversation, people tend to underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company. Researchers call it the liking gap.
In those studies, people were too wrapped up in worrying about what they'd said to notice the signs that the other person was enjoying it.
And then you see Juno.
She guessed you gave her a three. You gave her a nine.
Two people, both sure the other one wasn't interested. About to never talk again.
In one study of college roommates, that gap lasted for several months.
And remember how your chat ended? You said, I'll let you go.
In one study of nearly a thousand conversations, only about two percent ended when both people wanted them to.
She wasn't done talking. Neither were you.
Ten out of ten.

You'll never see the number. But after your next conversation, when your brain replays every awkward second, remember: they probably liked you more than you think. And if a conversation was good, you're allowed to keep it going.
Turns out, the only one giving you a two was you.
Weeks of awkward little waves. And never another real conversation.
Kai. You guess one.
So you go back.
The next day, you two talk for two hours.
